course: CMU 21-254: Linear Algebra and Vector Calculus for Engineers
title: Vectors, Dot Products, Magnitudes, and Angles
audience: SI leader teaching live on a whiteboard
toneRule: Keep explanations very simple, verbal, and board-friendly. Avoid textbook phrasing unless needed.
sessionGoal: Students should be able to do basic vector computations and explain what the dot product says about direction.
quickStartIfUnprepared: Remind students that vectors have size and direction.
Do Problem 1 to warm up components.
Do Problem 3 to connect dot product with perpendicular vectors.
sayThisFirst: A vector has size and direction.
The dot product gives a number, not another vector.
The dot product tells us how much two vectors point in the same direction.
If two vectors have dot product zero, they are perpendicular.
For points A and B, the vector from A to B is \(\overrightarrow{AB}=B-A\). Order matters.

boardPlan.whatToSay: These four formulas are enough for today. Most mistakes are notation or arithmetic, not concept.
Start with component arithmetic. Make them say out loud whether the answer should be a vector or a number.
Emphasize that \(\overrightarrow{AB}\) means start at A and end at B, so we do B minus A.
Use the dot product condition for perpendicular vectors. Then normalize the vector.
Ask students to name the three most important mistakes: wrong order for \(\overrightarrow{AB}\), forgetting squares in magnitude, and thinking dot product gives a vector.

keyFormulas.name: Magnitude
keyFormulas.plainEnglish: Magnitude is the length of the vector.

keyFormulas.name: Angle formula
keyFormulas.plainEnglish: This connects dot product to the angle between vectors.

keyFormulas.name: Vector from A to B
keyFormulas.plainEnglish: Endpoint minus start point. Order matters.

keyFormulas.name: Unit vector
keyFormulas.plainEnglish: Divide a nonzero vector by its length.

commonMistakes: Writing \(AB\) when you mean \(\overrightarrow{AB}\). Use the arrow.
Forgetting to square every component when finding magnitude.
Thinking the dot product gives a vector. It gives a scalar.
Saying vectors are perpendicular because they look perpendicular. Check the dot product.

notationWarnings.reason: AB usually names a segment or distance. The arrow tells students this is the vector from A to B.

problems.title: Component arithmetic and dot product
problems.studentPromptLatex: Let \(u=[3,-1,2]\) and \(v=[-2,4,1]\). Find \(2u-v\), compute \(u\cdot v\), find \(\|u\|\), and decide whether \(u\) and \(v\) are perpendicular.
problems.whatToSayBefore: Ask: which parts of this problem give vectors, and which parts give numbers?

boardSketchInstructions: Draw a small 3-column component table for x, y, z.
Put u and v in the first two rows.
Circle the fact that dot product is a scalar.
visualSpec.accuracyNote: This is an exact component table, not a geometric sketch.

walkthrough.label: Scale \(u\)
walkthrough.sayOutLoud: Scalar multiplication just multiplies every component.

walkthrough.label: Subtract \(v\)
walkthrough.sayOutLoud: Be careful with the minus sign on the first component: 6 minus negative 2 is 8.

walkthrough.label: Compute the dot product
walkthrough.sayOutLoud: The dot product is a number.

walkthrough.label: Check perpendicular
walkthrough.latex: u\cdot v=-8\ne 0,\quad \text{so }u\text{ and }v\text{ are not perpendicular.}
walkthrough.sayOutLoud: Perpendicular would mean dot product exactly zero.

commonMistakes: Stopping at \(u\cdot v=-8\) and saying perpendicular. It must be zero.

problems.title: From two points to a direction vector
skills: Vector from point A to point B
problems.studentPromptLatex: Let \(A=(1,-2,3)\) and \(B=(5,0,-1)\). Find \(\overrightarrow{AB}\), find the distance from \(A\) to \(B\), and find a unit vector pointing from \(A\) to \(B\).
problems.whatToSayBefore: The phrase 'from A to B' tells us the order: endpoint minus start point.

visualSpec.purpose: Show the vector from A to B as an arrow with the correct direction.
boardSketchInstructions: Mark A and B roughly, but do not spend too long on exact scale.
Draw an arrow starting at A and ending at B.
Write 'endpoint minus start point' next to the sketch.
visualSpec.accuracyNote: The coordinates and vector values are exact. The whiteboard drawing can be rough, but the arrow direction must be from A to B.

walkthrough.label: Use endpoint minus start point
walkthrough.sayOutLoud: Start at A, end at B, so use B minus A.

walkthrough.label: Subtract component by component
walkthrough.sayOutLoud: This is the direction and displacement from A to B.

walkthrough.label: Distance is the length of the vector
walkthrough.sayOutLoud: Distance between the points is the magnitude of the displacement vector.

walkthrough.label: Divide by the length to get a unit vector
walkthrough.sayOutLoud: A unit vector keeps the same direction but has length 1.

commonMistakes: Using \(A-B\), which points from B to A instead.
Forgetting to divide every component by 6 when making the unit vector.

problems.title: Choose a parameter to make vectors perpendicular
problems.studentPromptLatex: Let \(u=[2,1]\) and \(v=[k,8]\). Find \(k\) so that \(u\) and \(v\) are perpendicular. Then find a unit vector in the direction of \(v\).
problems.whatToSayBefore: When a problem says perpendicular, immediately think dot product equals zero.

visualSpec.purpose: Show the exact final vectors after solving for k.
boardSketchInstructions: After solving, draw \(v=[-4,8]\) from the origin.
Mark a right-angle symbol between the two directions.
visualSpec.accuracyNote: These two vectors are exactly perpendicular because \((2)(-4)+(1)(8)=0\).

walkthrough.label: Use the perpendicular condition
walkthrough.sayOutLoud: This is the main idea of the problem.

walkthrough.label: Find the length of \(v\)
walkthrough.sayOutLoud: We need the length before we can make a unit vector.

walkthrough.label: Divide by the length
walkthrough.sayOutLoud: This is the same direction as v, just length 1.

commonMistakes: Trying to use a picture before setting up the dot product.
Forgetting to plug \(k=-4\) back into \(v\) before finding the unit vector.

open.title: Two questions every vector answers
say: Welcome in. Before any formulas: a vector answers two questions. How long is it, and which way does it point?
Today we get a tool for comparing two vectors' directions without drawing anything: the dot product. By the end you'll be able to tell if two arrows are perpendicular just from their numbers.

ask.q: If I walk 3 blocks east and then 4 blocks north, how far am I from where I started?
ask.a: 5 blocks, by the Pythagorean theorem. That is exactly how we will measure vector length.

idea.title: The dot product measures how much two arrows agree
say: The dot product takes two vectors and gives back one number. That number is big and positive when the vectors point the same way, zero when they are perpendicular, and negative when they point against each other.
Why? Because \(\mathbf u\cdot\mathbf v=\|\mathbf u\|\|\mathbf v\|\cos\theta\). The lengths are never negative, so the sign comes entirely from \(\cos\theta\).
So a dot product of zero is the algebra version of a right angle. That is the one fact you will use all semester.
draw: Draw one fixed arrow u pointing right.
Draw three arrows v from the same point: one about 30° above u, one straight up, one about 150° around.
Under them write: dot product positive, zero, negative.
Shade the shadow of the first v on u and say: the dot product is the length of u times that shadow.

ask.q: What kind of object does a dot product give you: a vector or a number?
Two vectors have a dot product of −10. What can you say about the angle between them?
ask.a: It is more than 90°: cos θ is negative, so they point in generally opposite directions.

launch.say: Warm-up with every basic operation in one problem. As you work, label each answer: is it a vector or a number?
circulate: Look for 6 − (−2) written as 4. It is 8.
Check that the dot product answer is a single number, not a list.

askFirst.q: Which parts of this problem produce vectors and which produce numbers?
askFirst.a: 2u − v is a vector. u · v and ‖u‖ are numbers.

steps.say: Scalar multiplication multiplies every component. 2 times each entry.

ask.q: What does multiplying by 2 do to the arrow?

steps.say: Now subtract v component by component. First component: 6 minus negative 2, which is 8.
Dot product: multiply matching components, then add. (3)(−2) + (−1)(4) + (2)(1) = −6 − 4 + 2 = −8.

ask.q: The dot product is negative. What does that say about the angle between u and v?
ask.a: It is more than 90°; they point generally away from each other.

steps.why: The sign of the dot product tells you about the angle before you compute any angle.

steps.say: Length: square every component, add, take the square root. 9 + 1 + 4 = 14, so ‖u‖ = √14.

ask.q: Why do we square the −1 and not just use 1?
ask.a: (−1)² = 1 anyway, but the habit matters: every component gets squared, which is why length is never negative.

steps.say: Perpendicular means the dot product is exactly zero. We got −8, so they are not perpendicular.

ask.q: Could two vectors with a dot product of 0.001 be perpendicular?
ask.a: No. Perpendicular means exactly zero; 0.001 means the angle is very close to, but not exactly, 90°.

si01-p01.meaning: u and v point more than 90° apart, since their dot product is negative. The length √14 is how long the arrow u is in space.

ifStuck.if: a student writes the dot product as [−6, −4, 2]
ifStuck.then: ask what the last step of the dot product is: add the products. The answer is one number.

si01-p01.transition: So far the vectors were handed to us. Next, we build a vector from two points, and the order suddenly matters.

launch.say: Now we start from two points. Find the vector from A to B, the distance between them, and a unit vector in that direction.
circulate: Who computed A − B? Ask them which way their arrow points.
Check the unit vector: every component gets divided by 6.

askFirst.q: 'From A to B': which point do we start at, and which do we subtract?
askFirst.a: Start at A, end at B. Endpoint minus start point: B − A.

steps.say: From A to B means endpoint minus start point: B − A.

ask.q: What vector would A − B give?
ask.a: The same arrow pointing the other way, from B back to A.

steps.why: Order matters for displacement vectors. It will matter again for line integrals and orientation later in the course.

steps.say: Subtract one component at a time: 5 − 1, 0 − (−2), −1 − 3. That gives [4, 2, −4].

ask.a: To get from A to B you move 4 in x, 2 in y and −4 in z.

steps.say: The distance between the points is just the length of this vector: √(16 + 4 + 16) = √36 = 6.

ask.q: Why is the distance the same whether we used B − A or A − B?
ask.a: The two vectors are negatives of each other, and squaring removes the signs.

steps.say: To make a unit vector, divide every component by the length 6. The direction stays; the length becomes 1.

ask.q: How can you check a unit vector quickly?
ask.a: Its components' squares should add to 1: 4/9 + 1/9 + 4/9 = 1.

si01-p02.meaning: The displacement [4, 2, −4] carries both the distance (6) and the direction. The unit vector keeps only the direction, which is what you want when a problem asks which way something points.

ifStuck.if: a student divides only the first component by 6
ifStuck.then: ask them to check the length of their answer. It must come out to exactly 1.

si01-p02.transition: We've used the dot product to measure. Now we use it as an equation: pick a number that makes two vectors perpendicular.

launch.say: An exam-style twist: one component is unknown. Choose k so the vectors are perpendicular, then make a unit vector.
circulate: Who went straight to u · v = 0? That's the move.
After finding k, check that they plug it back in before normalizing.

steps.say: The word perpendicular is your cue: the dot product is zero.

ask.q: Why does a zero dot product mean a right angle?
ask.a: u · v = ‖u‖‖v‖cos θ, and the lengths are not zero, so cos θ = 0 and θ = 90°.

steps.say: Multiply matching components and add: 2 · k + 1 · 8 = 2k + 8.

ask.a: A number that depends on k. We will choose k to make it zero.

steps.say: Set it equal to zero: 2k = −8, so k = −4. Now v = [−4, 8].
Divide by 4√5: the unit vector is [−1/√5, 2/√5].

ask.q: Is this still perpendicular to u?
ask.a: Yes. Scaling a vector does not change its direction, so it is still perpendicular to u.

si01-p03.meaning: k = −4 rotates v to exactly 90° from u. On the board: u points up and to the right at a shallow angle, v points up and to the left steeply, and they meet at a right angle.

ifStuck.if: a student tries to find k from a picture
ifStuck.then: set up the dot product first. Pictures check answers; algebra finds them.
ask what dot product value means perpendicular. It is 0, not 1.

wrap.write: Dot product → a number. Zero ⟺ perpendicular. Length = √(v · v). From A to B = B − A. Unit vector = v / ‖v‖.

exit.q: What does the dot product output: a scalar or a vector?
What dot product value means perpendicular?
What is the vector from A to B?
exit.a: B − A: endpoint minus start point.

exit.q: How do you turn a vector into a unit vector?
exit.a: Divide it by its length (it must be nonzero).

wrap.next: Next time: matrices. A matrix is a machine that takes in a vector and gives back a new one, and the dot product is how it does the work, row by row.
